## Solution

We evaluate the Cauchy principal value
$$I = \text{P.V.}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{xe^{ix}}{x^2-\pi^2}\,dx.$$

**Step 1: Partial fraction decomposition.**

$$\frac{x}{x^2-\pi^2}=\frac{1}{2}\!\left(\frac{1}{x-\pi}+\frac{1}{x+\pi}\right),$$

so
$$I = \frac{1}{2}\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{x-\pi}\,dx+\frac{1}{2}\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{x+\pi}\,dx.$$

**Step 2: Reduce to the standard integral $\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{iu}}{u}\,du$.**

For the first integral, substitute $u = x - \pi$:
$$\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{x-\pi}\,dx = \text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{i(u+\pi)}}{u}\,du = e^{i\pi}\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{iu}}{u}\,du = -\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{iu}}{u}\,du.$$

For the second, substitute $u = x + \pi$:
$$\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{x+\pi}\,dx = \text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{i(u-\pi)}}{u}\,du = e^{-i\pi}\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{iu}}{u}\,du = -\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{iu}}{u}\,du.$$

**Step 3: Evaluate the standard integral via contour integration.**

Consider $g(z)=e^{iz}/z$, which has a simple pole at $z=0$ with residue $1$. Integrate over the contour consisting of the real axis (indented by a small clockwise semicircle $C_\epsilon$ of radius $\epsilon$ above the origin) and the large semicircle $\Gamma_R$ in the upper half-plane. Since $e^{iz}$ decays in the upper half-plane, Jordan's lemma gives $\int_{\Gamma_R}\to 0$. No singularity lies inside the indented contour, so by Cauchy's theorem:

$$\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{x}\,dx + \int_{C_\epsilon}g(z)\,dz = 0.$$

The clockwise semicircle around the simple pole contributes $-i\pi\,\text{Res}(g,0)=-i\pi$, hence

$$\text{P.V.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{x}\,dx = i\pi.$$

**Step 4: Combine.**

$$I = \frac{1}{2}(-i\pi)+\frac{1}{2}(-i\pi) = -i\pi.$$

**Consistency check.** The real part of the integrand $\frac{x\cos x}{x^2-\pi^2}$ is odd, so its P.V. integral is $0$ (consistent with $\operatorname{Re}(-i\pi)=0$). The imaginary part $\frac{x\sin x}{x^2-\pi^2}$ is even, and its integral equals $-\pi=\operatorname{Im}(-i\pi)$, as expected.

$$\boxed{I = -\,i\pi}$$
